newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia spending cuts could prompt parliament row.
newsitem.headline: Russia spending cuts could prompt parliament row.

text.p: Dismal tax revenues may force the Russian government to slash spending across the board this year to keep reforms on track, opening the door to a new row with the conservative lower house of parliament.

The 1997 budget, approved after prolonged horse-trading and much debate, says the government must ask parliament to approve new, lower spending proposals if revenues are more than 10 percent below planned levels.
Government ministers now admit their original plans were unrealistic and, pointing to below-target revenues, they say lower spending is the only way to resolve the problems.
Plans on sequestration -- cutting spending levels -- could be presented this month.
"Tax collection is lower not only compared to the budget, but also compared to last year," said Yevsei Gurvich, an economist with the Finance Ministry's Economic Expert Group.
He said March revenue was flat from March last year at around 80 percent of planned levels and added: "We just hope the situation will not be as bad as at the start of the year."

New ministers appointed by President Boris Yeltsin last month have promised to kick-start stalled economic reforms in an effort to revive the economy and win financial backing from the International Monetary Fund, which has already delayed several loan payments to Russia because of the low revenues.
The reformers highlight restructuring and anti-inflationary policies as the route to sustained growth.

News agencies said the economy would top the agenda at a meeting between Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin. Both have described low tax payments and high wage arrears as their biggest economic headaches.

But plans for lower spending to offset the lower revenues will reopen the bitter arguments of the last budget round, when deputies in the State Duma lower house slammed the government for unrealistic plans and demanded cash to help firms and individuals who lost out when reforms got under way.

"The finance ministry has to adopt a plan, and the Duma has to accept or reject it," said Roland Nash, chief economist at Renaissance Capital. "It means a whole new budget round -- a smaller one, but a new round nontheless."
Duma chairman Gennady Seleznyov said on Tuesday that Chernomyrdin would brief the lower house on the first quarter budget on April 23.
The Duma, elected in December 1995, is dominated by communists and their conservative allies, while the latest changes have given the government a more reformist bent.

Analysts said lower spending and a more realistic budget could help Russia out of its lengthy economic slump, provided the new government team held to its ambitious plans to reform and restructure the long-suffering economy.

"If they can manage to hang things together this year and keep inflation under control, one would expect the economy to start to pick up this year," said Vladimir Konovalov, chief economist at the World Bank in Moscow.
"We are hoping that we will start to see some kind of a turnaround."
